Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The United States takes the floor today to explain our no vote on eight of the resolutions considered today, specifically resolution one, Information from non-self-governing territories transmitted under Article 73e of the Charter of the United Nations. Resolution 2, economic and other activities which affect the interests of the peoples of the non-self-governing territories. Resolution 3, implementation of the declaration on the granting of independence to colonial countries and peoples by the specialized agencies and the international institutions associated with the United Nations. Resolution 4, question of American Samoa. Resolution 10, question of Guam. Resolution 17, question of the United States Virgin Islands. Resolution 18, dissemination of information on decolonization. And resolution 19, implementation of the declaration on the granting of independence to colonial countries and peoples. We vote no because of several longstanding concerns that we repeat year after year. The United States supports the right of peoples to self-determination. We will continue to uphold the full application of Article 73 of the UN Charter. However, we must reiterate our well-known concerns. These resolutions continue to place too much weight on independence as a one-size-fits-all status option for a territory's people in pursuit of their right to self-determination, as correctly stated by the Declaration on Principles of International Law Concerning Friendly Relations of 1970. The people of a non-self-governing territory may, as an alternative to independence, validly opt free association or any other political status, including integration with the administering state, provided the people freely determine such status. In other words, territories can speak for themselves. It is not for this Assembly to press any particular outcome. Leaving the decision, whatever it may be, to the free will of the people is the essence of the right of self-determination. Furthermore, the US government has a sovereign right to carry out its military activities in accordance with its national security interests. It is simplistic to assume military presence is necessarily harmful to the rights and interests of the people of a territory or incompatible with their wishes. With respect to the resolution on information from non-self-governing territories transmitted under Article 73E of the Charter, we underscore that it is for administering states to determine whether a territory has achieved self-governance under the terms of the Charter and whether to transmit information under Article 73E of the Charter. Regarding the resolution entitled the question of Guam, we again express disagreement with the criticism of a US federal court ruling, which enjoined Guam's planned plebiscite on self-determination. According to the US court's ruling, which was affirmed on appeal in 2019, the Guamanian law established the plebiscite violates US constitutional guarantees against race-based restrictions on the exercise of voting rights. The United States has long supported the right of self-determination for the people of Guam and continues to do so. We also find it necessary to reiterate the long-standing U.S. view that the right of self-determination of the people of a non-self-governing territory is to be exercised by the whole people, not just one portion of the population. Finally, we reiterate by reference the other concerns we have expressed in past years about these resolutions. We stress that these statements in these resolutions, as well as those in prior resolutions of the General Assembly, including Resolution 1514 of 1960, are non-binding and do not necessarily state or reflect international law. And any reaffirmation of prior documents in these resolutions applies only to those states which affirmed them initially. Additionally, the United States remains concerned by the reaffirmations of the 2030 agenda and the sustainable development goals. The 2030 agenda and...

Good morning to you, Mr. Chairman. The draft resolution that has just been adopted is rooted in resolution 1514. 15 and other relevant resolutions of the General Assembly on decolonization. As such, the applicability of this resolution to a specific territory depends on the idea that the principle of self-determination is actually applicable on that territory specifically. The right to self-determination requires, in order to be exercised, an active subject that is a people subject to subjugation, domination, or exploitation by a foreign power, according to the provisions of operative paragraph 1 of Resolution 1514, and a population that is ethnic and culturally distinct to the occupying power, in accordance with Resolution 1541, of of the General Assembly. If that subject does not exist, it is not appropriate to apply the principle of self-determination. This is the case with the Malvinas, South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands and the surrounding maritime areas. These are illegally occupied by the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. They expelled the population and the legitimate Argentine authorities and replaced them with British nationals. This fact makes the right to self-determination inapplicable to the question of the Malvinas Islands. That was recognized in all resolutions of the General Assembly on the Malvinas question, in particular resolution 2065/20 and those adopted to date by the Special Committee on Decolonization. In those texts, it was clearly established that, given that there is a sovereignty dispute at play, the way of putting an end to that colonial situation, that special and particular colonial situation was a negotiated solution to the dispute between the two parties, the United Kingdom and the Argentine Republic. They ruled out the application of the principle of self-determination. Moreover, in 1985, the General Assembly explicitly ruled out the applicability of the principle of self-determination to the question of the Malvinas Islands when it rejected by a vast majority two British proposals that sought to incorporate that principle into the specific draft resolution on the matter. The draft resolution adopted is not consequently applicable to the issue of the Malvinas Islands. It is appropriate to indicate that resolution 31/49 of the General Assembly urges Argentina and the United Kingdom to abstain from adopting decisions that lead to the adoption of unilateral modifications to the situation while the islands are under a negotiation process, as recommended by the General Assembly. Consequently, the unilateral exploration and exploitation by the UK of natural resources in the Malvinas Islands, South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands and the surrounding maritime areas run counter to that resolution and prejudge the result of the sovereignty dispute. Thank you.

Thank you, Chair. As this is the first time Australia is taking the floor, I would like to congratulate you and the Bureau on your election and assure you of Australia's cooperation and support. Chair, Australia is a proud supporter of the right of peoples of non-self-governing territories to self-determination in accordance with international law, including the UN Charter. As we have in previous years, Australia abstained from this resolution due to the retention in operative paragraph 13 of a call to terminate all military activities and eliminate military bases in non-self-governing territories. Australia recognises the obligation of nations to promote the wellbeing of those in the territories they administer, as enshrined in the UN Charter. We do not believe that taking action to defend such territories necessarily runs counter to those obligations or the interests of the people in those territories. In many cases, such action serves to advance international peace and security, an important consideration in Article 73 of the UN Charter, which is dedicated to promoting the interests of the inhabitants of non-self-governing territories. In our Pacific region, many countries work together to address shared challenges. In an increasingly disaster-prone region, military support plays a key role in delivering critical humanitarian assistance and disaster relief. The same military cooperation promotes maritime security, providing further benefits to the region and its people. In abstaining from this resolution, Australia joins other countries in affirming OP 13 remains unacceptable and, in our view, it should be removed from further iterations of this text. Thank you.

Distinguished delegate of Mongolia, you can do a voting intention via e-delegate. My colleagues to the left at the table are happy to assist you in order to do so because the voting was completed. Thank you.
I give the floor now to the distinguished representative of Argentina.

Thank you very much, Chair, once again. My country wishes to recall that the visiting missions are only appropriate in the case of territories for which the United Nations has recognized that the principle of self-determination is applicable. The doctrine of the Special Committee on Decolonization itself is clear in this regard. It states that such missions are not appropriate for territories in which there is a sovereignty dispute recognized by the United Nations, a position that has been endorsed by regional seminars. They have been excluded, those visiting missions, on the same grounds. This is also in line with statements saying that visiting missions must be deployed on a case-by-case basis and must be deployed in accordance with the relevant resolutions of the United Nations. That is fully in line with resolution 859. That resolution establishes that, for a visiting mission to take place, there must be the approval of the General Assembly for that deployment to occur.

I thank the distinguished delegation of Argentina.

I see no further requests for the floor. The Committee has thus concluded its consideration of agenda item 58. The Committee will now resume its consideration of agenda item 59, entitled Eradicating colonialism in all its forms and manifestations. The Committee has before it a draft resolution containing document A/C4/80/L.5, entitled "International Day against Colonialism in all its Forms and Manifestations." I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela. To introduce draft resolution A/C.4/80/L.5.

Chair, thank you very much. The Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela is honored to take the floor on behalf of the Group of Friends in Defense of the Charter of the United Nations as co-penholder of the draft resolution entitled International Day Against Colonialism in all its Forms and Manifestations. contained in document A/C4/80/L5. This initiative has its very raison d'etre in the collective commitment to the United Nations Charter and our commitment to the implementation of resolution 1514/15 of the General Assembly, dated 1960. That resolution contains the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples. Sixty-five years after its option, the international community must acknowledge that decolonization has yet to be achieved. Many peoples continue to face forms of foreign domination, occupation and interference that prevent the full enjoyment of their inalienable right to self-determination. The draft resolution drafted in a procedural fashion reaffirms the relevance of that historic declaration and other related instruments. It recognizes, moreover, that colonialism persists in its traditional forms and through new manifestations that undermine sovereignty and perpetuate dependency. Once adopted, it will make it possible to promote historical realities and the modern realities of colonialism. It will make it possible to honour colonialism's victims and encourage reparative justice and non-repetition. Chair, this initiative is underpinned by a constructive, inclusive spirit and is future-oriented. It does not seek to examine divisions, but rather to reaffirm shared responsibility responsibilities and principles. The Group of Friends in Defence of the Charter of the United Nations is grateful to delegations that actively and constructively participated in the negotiation of that draft, and we thank those that supported it with their co-sponsorship. We hope that the Fourth Committee, in line with its traditional practice and mandate, will adopt this draft resolution by consensus, and we urge all its members, should a vote occur, to vote in favour of the text contained in the document. Voting in favour of that text will be to vote in favour of history, justice and solidarity. It will be a vote to complete one of the oldest and as yet unfulfilled mandates of the United Nations, that is, the complete eradication of colonialism in all its forms and manifestations. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

I thank the distinguished representative of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela.

We shall now consider draft resolution A/C.4/80/L.5. I give the floor to the Secretary to announce the additional co-sponsors of draft resolution L.5.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. The additional co-sponsors on the e-delegate portal of the Fourth Committee are reflected on the screen. Delegations not reflected on the screen wishing to co-sponsor draft resolution L.5, please signify by pressing the microphone button now to be added to the list of co-sponsors. I see no additional co-sponsors. Thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the Secretary. I open the floor to delegations wishing to make general statements or explain their vote before the vote. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Morocco.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. The Kingdom of Morocco wishes to deliver this explanation of vote to reaffirm our position regarding the process of the negotiations of the resolution entitled International Day Against Colonialism in all its forms and manifestations, as previously expressed in our letter L-130-2025 of 13 October 2025, sent to all UN member states. Morocco has consistently demonstrated its commitment to multilateralism and has always actively participated in negotiations with a spirit of dialogue, mutual respect and constructive engagement. In that same spirit, we participated in the consultations on this draft resolution with a sincere aim of contributing to a balanced, inclusive and consensual outcome that reflects the views and concerns of the wider membership. However, we must express our deep regret over the conduct of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela in its capacity as co-facilitator of this process. Contrary to the principles of transparency, neutrality and constructiveness that are expected of facilitators in multilateral settings, the approach adopted by Venezuela fell short of these standards. Morocco's substantive inputs, including key textual amendments, were either overlooked or misrepresented in both the first and second revision of the draft text. Moreover, Morocco formally broke silence on Rev 2, signaling serious concerns with the direction of the draft. Despite this clear indication, there was no attempt by the co-facilitator to re-engage, open dialogue, or seek any form of compromise. Instead, the revised text was unilaterally tabled without any notification to delegations that Morocco had broken silence. Such actions represent a clear departure from established negotiation practices and undermine the spirit of trust and cooperation that should guide our collective work. We stress once again that genuine facilitation requires openness and a commitment to consensus building. It is unfortunate that this process was driven forward in a manner that excluded and disregarded legitimate concerns raised by member states. With this approach, Venezuela undermines the credibility of our multilateral processes and sets a concerning example for future negotiations. Despite these challenges, Morocco acknowledges the constructive role played by another delegation amongst the co-authors of the text, which sought to maintain dialogue and bridge divergent views in the days leading to the resolution's examination. In particular, we would like to sincerely thank the Russian Federation for their active efforts to narrow down differences and promote a more inclusive approach. Such is the engagement that should have prevailed throughout the process, one that preserves a measure of openness and the value of responsible diplomacy. I thank you, Mr. Chair.

I thank the distinguished representative of Morocco. I see no further requests for the floor. The Committee will now take a decision on draft resolution A/C.4/80/L.5, entitled International Day Against Colonialism in all its Forms and Manifestations. A recorded vote has been requested. We shall now begin the voting process. Those in favour of draft resolution L.5, please signify. Those against? Abstentions.

The Committee is now voting on draft resolution L.5, entitled "International Day against Colonialism in all its Forms and Manifestations". Will all delegations confirm that their votes are accurately reflected on the screen? The voting has been completed. Please lock the machine.

The result of the vote is as follows. In favor, 101. Against, 2. Abstentions, 51. Draft resolution A/C.4/80/L.5 is adopted. I now open the floor for delegations wishing to explain their vote after the vote or make general statements. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation.

Mr. Chairman. We were one of the co-sponsors of this resolution on the establishment of an International Day against Colonialism in all its forms and manifestations. As such, the Russian Federation extends its gratitude to all those who supported the delegation to all such to the resolutions at the year of the anniversary of the granting of independence to colonial countries and peoples. The adoption of this document is an important step on the path to implementing the noble goals of this historic document and the need to immediately and unconditionally end colonialism in all its forms and manifestations. Despite the elimination of colonial empires and the creation of more durable states in the next half of the 20th century, Speaking of the full victory over colonialism, unfortunately, it is still premature. The repercussions of this phenomenon are felt all throughout the globe and still hamper the full development of sovereign states. We note the fact that, thanks to the adoption on the initiative of the Group of Friends in Defense of the UN Charter, of resolution 79/150. At the current session of the Fourth Committee, for the first time, we for the first time and very successfully debated this new agenda item on the eradication of colonialism in all of its forms. We trust that we will continue this discussion, including in the context of holding commemorative events to celebrate the new International Day this year already. Thank you for your attention.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Indonesia voted in favor of this draft resolution as a reflection of our long-standing and unwavering commitment to efforts to end colonialism. As my delegation underlined during the general debate, the call to end colonialism is embedded as part of Indonesia's DNA. The spirit of Bandung Principles continues to guide us, that no people shall live under subjugation. At the same time, Indonesia believes that this noble cause must never be politicized or manipulated to advance separatist agendas that undermine the sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity of member states. In this regard, our delegation underscores that the observance of the International Day against Colonialism must maintain the intergovernmental nature of decolonization process and remain consistent with OP1 of the resolution. It should be in full conformity with the spirit and letter of the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and People, and the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, including respect to sovereignty and territorial integrity of all Member States. The International Day must serve as a platform for all Member States to advance decolonization agenda under the mandate of the Fourth Committee and the C24 for the remaining 17 non-self-governing territories. Mr. Chair, in the spirit of reform of the multilateral system as a whole, including to support the UN80 initiative, we must ensure that all of our efforts should be directed for a more efficient and effective United Nations. My delegation would like to emphasize that we must avoid any duplications of initiatives, including on the establishment of a new international day. Therefore, it is our sincere wish that the observance of this International Day against Colonialism will be a moment of solidarity for making the United Nations a place for all to stand united against all forms of colonialism while upholding sovereignty, equality, and integrity of every nation. I thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Indonesia. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United States.

Mr. Chairman, the United States requested a recorded vote on this resolution and is voting no for the following reasons. First, the United States generally opposes the creation of new international days in the UN system. They add unnecessary costs and work to an already overloaded and costly UN agenda, costs and work that member states must bear. This resolution, for example, proposes a new yearly General Assembly debate, including participation by the Secretary-General and the President of the General Assembly. Such efforts duplicate work already underway in the Fourth Committee and the General Assembly. Furthermore, we question the drafter and co-sponsors' intentions with this resolution. Though this is disguised as a decolonization initiative, statements by Venezuela and Russia on October 3 indicate otherwise. They have made clear they are actually raising a number of unrelated accusations against the United States and other member states under this new agenda item. Second, we note the contradiction between this resolution and the actions of the drafter and certain cosponsors. We question their putting forward resolutions espousing territorial integrity when they are taking actions inconsistent with that principle. Both the drafter, Venezuela, and one of the co-sponsors, Russia, are taking actions that threaten or infringe the sovereignty of neighboring states. Venezuela has sought to escalate its territorial dispute with Guyana. Russia, enabled by another co-sponsor, Belarus, continues to occupy Ukrainian territory and to conduct a devastating war in Ukraine. These actions, when considered against the backdrop of this resolution, raise more questions about the intent behind it. Third, this resolution calls for the pursuit of reparations based on flawed narratives. These suggestions pose a significant financial burden that taxpayers of member states would ultimately pay. The United States categorically rejects this concept and steadfastly opposes this resolution. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of the United States.

I now give the floor to the distinguished delegation of Mexico.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Mexico voted in favour of resolution L5 in line with its historic commitment to the principle of self-determination of peoples and our commitment to addressing unresolved decolonization issues. These are fundamental issues in the way my country conducts itself within the multilateral system, there are also principles enshrined in our constitution. However, we wish to place on record our position regarding the proclamation of new international days and years. Despite the fact that these commemorative celebrations have symbolic value, they have also produced a significant operational and financial burden. We are of the view that issues related to these days can and must be implemented through substantive mechanisms and continuing ones, without as necessarily requiring the proclamation of an international day. In the previous General Assembly session, 11 days and one international year were proclaimed. In the previous session, 15 days and six international years were declared. And in the 77th session, 12 international days and two international years were proclaimed. This trend was recognized appropriately with concern in resolution 179/327 on the revitalization of the work of the General Assembly. Through that text, all member states agreed that we would suspend the examination of new proposals to proclaim international days and years during the 81st session and 82nd session. That would be a test exercise. We agreed to group these initiatives under thematic frameworks. The fact that their implementation has not yet begun must not be interpreted as an opportunity to adopt a higher number of new commemorative celebrations in this session. On the contrary, this is an appropriate juncture within the initiative of UN80 to demonstrate a collective commitment to more streamlined, efficient and coherent management of the work of this Assembly. As such, Mexico is of the view that it is necessary to move towards a more efficient, coherent and thematically integrated mechanism and to ensure that these initiatives have added value for the work of the United Nations. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Mexico.

To the distinguished representative of Poland.

Mr. Chair, Belgium, Czechia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Kingdom of the Netherlands, Republic of Moldova, Romania, and my country, Poland. decided to abstain on the resolution on International Day against Colonialism in all its forms and manifestations. Our position on colonialism is well known and does not have to be repeated here. Nonetheless, we have decided to abstain on this resolution, considering the following facts. In July this year, the General Assembly adopted resolution 79/318 on Secretary-General's UN initiative. The text, which has been agreed by consensus, stresses the need for strengthening the impact of the UN and enhancing its agility, responsiveness and resilience, while addressing the issue of duplicative efforts and ensuring effective and efficient mandate delivery across all three pillars of the work of the UN. In September this year, through resolution 79/327 on revitalization of the work of the General Assembly, UN members expressed their concern about the significant increase in the number of proposals to proclaim international days, weeks, months, and years. In December 2020, resolution 75/123 dedicated to the fourth decade for the eradication of colonialism was adopted. In December 2019, the GA passed resolution 74/113, whereby it already requested the Special Committee to adopt necessary measures to observe annually the Week of Solidarity with the Peoples of Non-Self-Governing Territories. Mr. Chair, instead of announcing new initiatives, the UN should focus on implementation of existing declarations and provisions. In this context, we look forward to the UN Secretary-General's report on implementation of the above-mentioned resolution 75 that is scheduled to be delivered during this session of the General Assembly. There is a strong feeling in this room, among the majority of the Member States, on the need to make the UN more effective. How can we expect the UN80 initiative to deliver meaningful solutions if we engage in promotion of new political initiatives that only duplicate existing mechanisms and do not offer any new and useful solutions? The UN should concentrate on practical actions, not on empty political declarations. Mr. Chair, last but not least, it is a tragic paradox and a clear example of hypocrisy that Russia, an aggressor with evident neocolonial ambitions both in its immediate neighborhood and in other parts of the world, is among the co-sponsors of the project we are voting on today. Among tragic victims of Russia's colonialism remain also the oppressed Bashkirs, Circassians, Kalmyks, Buryats, Tuvans, and other peoples within Russia. These groups continue to endure ethnic, linguistic, and cultural eradication, now even further compounded by forced conscription of their male population for the ongoing war effort against Ukraine. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Poland. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Australia.

Thank you, Chair. I have the honor to deliver this explanation of vote on behalf of Canada, New Zealand, and my own country, Australia. Cairns members are strong supporters of the right of all peoples to self-determination. We will continue to promote the full implementation of Article 73 of the UN Charter. Cairns continues to work across the United Nations decolonization agenda. We abstained from voting on this resolution for three reasons. First, there are already a number of existing resolutions on colonization under consideration by the Fourth Committee. Second, the resolution contains proposals that go against the spirit and intent of the UN 80 initiative and the UN General Assembly revitalization process. The Secretary-General's UN 80 mandate report of 12th of May 2025 called for ways to avoid duplication and ensure strategic use of resources across the UN system. The General Assembly Revitalization Resolution noted with concern the significant increase in the number of proposals to proclaim international days and called for restraint on new mandates. Cairns shares these concerns regarding the proliferation of international days and their resource implications. Third, this resolution is being introduced by a sponsor whose voting rights are currently suspended in the General Assembly. Chair, it must also be restated in this committee that one of the co-sponsors of the resolution, a permanent member of the UN Security Council, is actively undermining the decolonization agenda by waging an illegal war to reassert imperial control over an independent sovereign state. Russia's illegal war of aggression undermines the UN Charter, which prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. Our collective commitments to uphold sovereignty and territorial integrity are intrinsic to decolonization. Chair, Cairns remains open to good faith discussions on innovative solutions to the complex issues of self-determination. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Australia. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom.

Mr. Chairman, I'd like to briefly explain the vote of the United Kingdom on this issue. When considering any proposal to establish a new international day, we've got to be conscious of the priority that UN bodies and member states are rightly placing on ensuring the UN is more efficient, cost-effective, and sustainable. Furthermore, any proposed international day should fulfil the basic purpose of commemorating issues which unite Member States. As last year's vote on resolution A/79/115 demonstrated, this issue does not carry the full support of the room. Indeed, this resolution has been crafted instead to be divisive. The failure of this resolution to satisfy either of these considerations, even before serious consideration is given to the detail of the resolution, compels the UK to abstain. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Austria.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chair. Austria abstained on draft resolution L5, entitled International Day Against Colonialism in All Its Forms and Manifestations. Permit me a few moments to explain why. Austria recognizes the profound and lasting impact that colonialism, in all its forms and manifestations, has had on countries and societies across the world. Throughout the decades of its membership in the United Nations, Austria has therefore supported efforts aimed at overcoming colonialism and its legacy, advancing the right to self-determination and promoting remembrance, as also exemplified by our positions on many resolutions under agenda items 54 to 58 today. Since joining the United Nations in 1955, Austria has taken a principled stance in favor of decolonization and the peaceful resolution of disputes, guided by the belief that freedom, equality, and cooperation among sovereign nations are the foundation of international peace and security. Austria's approach has always emphasized constructive engagement and the importance of learning from history to build a more just and inclusive international order. This understanding was also the basis of Austria's support to General Assembly Resolution 1514, containing the declaration on the granting of independence to colonial countries and peoples in 1960, and Austria's support to resolutions proclaiming the international decades for the eradication of colonialism, most recently through Resolution 75/123 in December 2020. However, we regret that some of the main sponsors of draft resolution L5 tried to give this initiative a different context. Austria would therefore like to put on record that we understand the proclamation of the International Day Against Colonialism in all its forms and manifestations as a continuation of the United Nations' important efforts on decolonization as laid out in General Assembly resolution 1514, which Austria supported. We would also like to underline that our common efforts regarding the topic of decolonization must be guided by our shared commitment to the principles and purposes of the UN Charter, the respect for human rights and the rule of law. In view of the above, while Austria shares the objective of fully implementing General Assembly resolution 1514, we abstained on draft resolution L5. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Austria.

I thank the distinguished representative of Spain.

The distinguished representative of Germany.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Germany abstained on the resolution entitled International Day Against Colonialism in All Its Forms and Manifestations. During the colonial era, Germany was among the countries that caused immense suffering in various parts of the world. We recognize our historical responsibility. In recent years, public awareness in Germany about the crimes and atrocities committed during the colonial period and their lasting consequences has grown significantly. This awareness has led to concrete policies aimed at addressing the legacies of colonialism. This includes supporting independent academic research into Germany's colonial past, as well as naming and recognizing the injustices that have been committed. For example, based on our strong and cordial relationship, Germany and Namibia have initiated a political dialogue to address the atrocities committed by German colonial troops against the OvaHerrero and Nama communities from 1904 to 1908, atrocities that resulted in genocide. Federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier as well, during his visit to Tanzania in 2023, asked for forgiveness for Germany's colonial crimes. German museums actively research the provenance of their artifacts, and some of these have been returned to their countries of origin in consultation with the affected communities. When addressing our colonial past, it is essential for us to do so in dialogue with the governments, societies, and diaspora of former colonies. Open discussion and mutual listening are the only ways to build authentic partnerships and to overcome the colonial legacy. Mr. Chair, for Germany, confronting the legacies of colonialism remains a critical and ongoing priority. It is against this background that we regret that we were not able to support this resolution. With the introduction of this agenda item, we believe there is a duplication of processes, both within the Fourth Committee and with regard to the Third Committee. Moreover, we share the concerns raised by Poland and many other Member States about the motive of one of the sponsors of this resolution, a UN Member State that has been waging a war of aggression against a neighboring country for over three years. We would strongly recommend that this Member State embrace PP9 of the resolution, which states, reaffirming that any attempt aimed at the partial or total disruption of the national unity and territorial integrity of a country is incompatible with the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations." This member state seeks to present itself as an advocate of decolonization and an opponent of imperialism. Yet, it simultaneously justifies its aggression using a profoundly imperialist rationale, claiming a sphere of influence over sovereign nations and denying them the sovereign right to make their own decisions regarding alliances and governance. Therefore, we cannot consider this endeavor a fully credible contribution to addressing the legacy of colonialism. I thank you, Mr. Chair.
